explain.english-grammar-5068: "Dormant" means inactive or in a sleep-like state, as an animal is when hibernating; the other options mean lively or active.
explain.english-grammar-5069: A "peer" is a person of the same age, rank or standing, i.e. a fellow or equal.
explain.english-grammar-5163: A "knack" is a special skill or ability for doing something well.
explain.english-grammar-5694: To "elope" means to run away secretly with a lover, usually in order to marry.
explain.english-grammar-5852: Documents such as photographs are "attached" to an application form; "hook up", "fix" and "link" are not idiomatic here.
explain.english-grammar-5853: To "live off" something means to rely on it as one's only source of food or support, as in living off juice.
explain.english-grammar-5855: The verb "deprive" takes the preposition "of": to deprive someone of something.
explain.english-grammar-5864: Something that is inside a pocket is found "in" the pocket.
explain.english-grammar-5880: "Whose" is the possessive relative pronoun needed here: Javed, two of whose brothers attend school.
explain.english-grammar-5882: "Concerned with" means involved in or connected with; "not concerned with his affairs" means having no involvement in them.
explain.english-grammar-5883: Money is "spent" on something; "did spend" is the emphatic past form.
explain.english-grammar-5886: "Come across" means to meet or find someone by chance.
explain.english-grammar-5931: "Advice" is uncountable, so it takes "some", not "one" or "an".
explain.english-grammar-5933: "Remember me to someone" is an idiom meaning please give that person my greetings.
explain.english-grammar-5938: A preposition such as "at" is followed by a gerund, so "good at speaking" is correct.
explain.english-grammar-5951: "Few" means not many (with a negative sense), which suits the contrast introduced by "but".
explain.english-grammar-5952: A third conditional (If + past perfect) takes "would have + past participle" in the result clause: would not have been disqualified.
explain.english-grammar-5954: "Call it a day" is an idiom meaning to stop work for the time being.
explain.english-grammar-5956: "Excessive" means more than is normal or healthy, which fits too much weight gain or loss.
explain.english-grammar-5957: "Transparent" is the standard term for a system that is open and easy for citizens to access and understand.
explain.english-grammar-5968: "Me" receives the action of the verb "called", so it is an object pronoun.
explain.english-grammar-6056: "Would you like to ...?" is the polite fixed form for making an invitation.
explain.english-grammar-6057: "Possess" means to have or own; human beings possess latent power.
explain.english-grammar-6234: "Yesterday" marks a finished past time, so the simple past "died" is required.
explain.english-grammar-6258: "From now on" refers to the future, so the future negative "won't" is needed.
explain.english-grammar-6259: "Yesterday" indicates a completed past action, which takes the simple past "saw".
explain.english-grammar-6281: "Wish + would" expresses a desire for someone to do something in the future: I wish Sana would come soon.
explain.english-grammar-7022: A bangle is worn on the wrist, which is part of the arm near the hand; likewise an anklet is worn on the ankle, near the foot.
explain.english-grammar-7024: "Abstruse" means difficult to understand; punctilious means careful about details and obtuse means slow-witted.
explain.english-grammar-7025: "King" is a general name for any ruler of that kind, so it is a common noun.
explain.english-grammar-7146: In the passive, the indirect object "him" becomes the subject "He", and the doer is introduced with "by": He was asked a question by Mr. Jamal.
explain.english-grammar-7152: A clock time takes "at" (at three o'clock) and a purpose takes "for" (for tea).
explain.english-grammar-7166: "Have trouble" is followed by a gerund: have trouble sleeping.
explain.islamic-gk-5299: On arriving in Madinah the Prophet stayed in the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, where his camel knelt, until his own quarters beside the mosque were built.
explain.islamic-gk-5323: During his final illness the Prophet instructed that Abu Bakr lead the people in prayer, and Abu Bakr led the congregational prayers in the Prophet's Mosque.
explain.islamic-gk-5333: After the death of his mother Aminah, the young Prophet was cared for by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib until Abd al-Muttalib died when the Prophet was about eight.
explain.islamic-gk-5335: Halimah al-Sadiyyah of the Banu Sa'd nursed and raised the infant Prophet in the desert, making her his best-known foster mother.
explain.islamic-gk-5337: Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's uncle martyred at Uhud, was given the title Asadullah, the Lion of Allah.
explain.islamic-gk-5357: Zaynab, the eldest daughter of the Prophet and Khadijah, was married to Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi.
explain.islamic-gk-6492: Ummah means a community or nation; in Islam it refers to the community of believers united by a shared faith.
explain.islamic-gk-6526: The Quran states that it was revealed in the month of Ramadan (Al-Baqarah 2:185), beginning on Laylat al-Qadr.
explain.islamic-gk-6527: The fast begins at true dawn (subh sadiq, the start of Fajr) and ends at sunset (Maghrib), as stated in Al-Baqarah 2:187.
explain.islamic-gk-6544: Zakat on gold, silver, cash and trade goods held above the nisab for a lunar year is due at one-fortieth, i.e. 2.5 percent.
explain.islamic-gk-7219: Abu Bakr governed from Madinah, which remained the capital throughout the Rashidun caliphate until Ali moved to Kufa.
explain.islamic-gk-7223: In 9 AH the Prophet appointed Abu Bakr as amir of the Hajj, and Ali was later sent to proclaim the opening verses of Surah Al-Tawbah.
explain.islamic-gk-7224: The Prophet had prepared an army under Usamah ibn Zayd before his death, and Abu Bakr insisted on dispatching it immediately after becoming caliph.
explain.islamic-gk-7226: Umar ibn al-Khattab succeeded Abu Bakr in 13 AH as the second Rightly Guided Caliph.
explain.islamic-gk-7228: Umar became caliph on Abu Bakr's death in 13 AH and ruled until he was assassinated in 23 AH, about ten years.
explain.islamic-gk-7229: Umar was the first caliph to be addressed as Amir al-Mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful), and the title became standard thereafter.
explain.islamic-gk-7231: Under Umar the Muslims chose the year of the Prophet's Hijrah to Madinah (622 CE) as year one of the Islamic calendar.
explain.islamic-gk-7249: Uthman was chosen caliph in 23 AH after Umar's death and was martyred in 35 AH, a rule of about twelve years.
explain.islamic-gk-7269: After the Battle of Siffin (37 AH) between Ali and Muawiyah, both sides agreed to arbitration, which led to the controversy and the Kharijite split.
explain.islamic-gk-7278: Hisbah is the duty of enjoining good and supervising markets and public morals, and the officer who carried it out was the muhtasib.
explain.islamic-gk-7284: Abu Bakr's personal name was Abdullah, son of Abu Quhafah (Uthman ibn Amir); Abu Bakr was his kunya and al-Siddiq his title.
explain.islamic-gk-7286: Abu Bakr bought Bilal from Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who was torturing him for his faith, and set him free.
explain.islamic-gk-7289: In his inaugural address Abu Bakr said: 'Obey me as long as I obey Allah and His Messenger; if I disobey them, you owe me no obedience.'
explain.islamic-gk-7298: The army of Usamah ibn Zayd, which the Prophet had prepared for the Byzantine frontier in Syria, was sent by Abu Bakr soon after he became caliph.
explain.islamic-gk-7301: After the Riddah wars Abu Bakr sent Khalid ibn al-Walid against the Persians in Iraq and armies against the Byzantines in Syria.

explain.islamic-gk-7343: Uthman bought the Well of Rumah from its owner and endowed it so that the Muslims of Madinah could draw water freely.
explain.islamic-gk-7351: The Battle of the Masts (Dhat al-Sawari), about 34-35 AH, was the first major Muslim naval victory over the Byzantine fleet, fought during Uthman's caliphate.
explain.islamic-gk-7352: As governor of Syria, Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan built the first Muslim navy, with Uthman's permission.

explain.islamic-gk-7359: Ali's father was Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's uncle who raised and protected him.
explain.islamic-gk-7374: At the arbitration after Siffin, Amr ibn al-As represented Muawiyah and Abu Musa al-Ashari represented Ali.
explain.islamic-gk-7375: A group of Ali's followers rejected the arbitration, saying 'judgement belongs to Allah alone', and broke away; they became known as the Kharijites.

explain.islamic-gk-7386: Surah Al-Nas is the 114th and final surah in the standard order of the Quran.
explain.islamic-gk-7389: Surah Al-Tawbah (Bara'ah), the ninth surah, is the only surah that does not begin with Bismillah in the mushaf.
explain.islamic-gk-7398: Al-Hijr 15:87 mentions 'seven of the oft-repeated' (al-sab' al-mathani), and authentic hadith identifies it as Surah Al-Fatihah.
explain.islamic-gk-7399: The command to fast in Ramadan is in Al-Baqarah 2:183-185.
explain.islamic-gk-7400: 'There is no compulsion in religion' is verse 256 of Surah Al-Baqarah.
explain.islamic-gk-7401: 'Hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not be divided' is Ali Imran 3:103.
explain.islamic-gk-7402: The fixed shares of inheritance are set out in Surah Al-Nisa, verses 11, 12 and 176.
explain.islamic-gk-7406: Surah Yusuf (Surah 12) tells the story of Prophet Yusuf as one continuous narrative.
explain.islamic-gk-7407: Surah Al-Isra (Surah 17) is also known as Bani Isra'il because it speaks about the Children of Israel.
explain.islamic-gk-7409: Surah Maryam (Surah 19) is named after Maryam, mother of Isa, and she is the only woman named in the Quran.
explain.islamic-gk-7410: The Verse of Light, 'Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth', is Al-Nur 24:35.
explain.islamic-gk-7412: Al-Ahzab 33:56 commands the believers to send blessings and peace upon the Prophet.
explain.islamic-gk-7416: Surah Al-Rahman repeats 'Which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?' 31 times.
explain.islamic-gk-7417: Surah Al-Waqiah opens with 'When the Inevitable Event (al-waqi'ah) occurs', a name for the Resurrection.
explain.islamic-gk-7419: Surah Al-Alaq opens with 'Iqra bismi rabbika' ('Read in the name of your Lord'), the first verses revealed.
explain.islamic-gk-7420: Surah Al-Qadr (97:3) states that the Night of Decree is better than a thousand months.
explain.islamic-gk-7421: Surah Al-Takathur begins: 'Competition in increase diverts you, until you visit the graves.'
explain.islamic-gk-7422: Surah Al-Asr says humankind is in loss except those who believe, do righteous deeds, and urge one another to truth and patience.
explain.islamic-gk-7423: Authentic hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says Surah Al-Ikhlas equals one-third of the Quran.
explain.islamic-gk-7427: Salat al-Khusuf is the prayer offered at a lunar eclipse; the prayer for a solar eclipse is usually called Salat al-Kusuf.
explain.islamic-gk-7430: Tahajjud is the voluntary night prayer offered after waking from sleep, commended in Al-Isra 17:79.
explain.islamic-gk-7431: Tarawih is the Ramadan night prayer, commonly offered in congregation after Isha.
explain.islamic-gk-7432: Witr means 'odd'; it is the prayer of an odd number of rakahs (such as one or three) offered at night after Isha.
explain.islamic-gk-7442: Ruku is the bowing position in prayer, where one bends with hands on the knees.
explain.islamic-gk-7450: Each Eid prayer consists of two rakahs offered in congregation with extra takbirs.
explain.islamic-gk-7451: The funeral prayer (Salat al-Janazah) is offered standing with takbirs only, and has no ruku or sujud.
explain.islamic-gk-7452: A congregation (jama'ah) is formed by at least two people, an imam and one follower, for ordinary prayers.
explain.islamic-gk-7456: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar.
explain.islamic-gk-7458: Dhul-Qadah is the eleventh month of the Islamic calendar, coming before Dhul-Hijjah.
explain.islamic-gk-7460: The Quran (Al-Tawbah 9:36) states that the number of months with Allah is twelve.

explain.islamic-gk-7462: The four sacred months are Muharram, Rajab, Dhul-Qadah and Dhul-Hijjah.
explain.islamic-gk-7463: Umar ibn al-Khattab introduced the Hijri calendar for official records, around 17 AH.
explain.islamic-gk-7470: The Prophet said that fasting Ramadan followed by six days of Shawwal is like fasting the whole year (Sahih Muslim).
explain.islamic-gk-7471: The 'white days' (Ayyam al-Bid) are the 13th, 14th and 15th of each lunar month, when the moon is full or nearly full.
explain.islamic-gk-7472: The Prophet regularly fasted on Mondays and Thursdays, saying that deeds are presented to Allah on those days.
explain.islamic-gk-7473: Suhur is the meal eaten before dawn by a person who intends to fast.
explain.islamic-gk-7474: Iftar is the meal taken at sunset to break the day's fast.
explain.islamic-gk-7475: Surah Al-Qadr says Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Decree, is better than a thousand months.
explain.islamic-gk-7481: Classical fiqh sets the nisab of silver at 200 dirhams (about 52.5 tolas) and the nisab of gold at 20 mithqals.
explain.islamic-gk-7490: Hawl is the passing of one full lunar year over wealth at or above the nisab, after which zakat becomes due.
explain.islamic-gk-7491: Ihram is the state of ritual consecration a pilgrim enters, with intention and prescribed clothing, before Hajj or Umrah.
explain.islamic-gk-7493: Dhul-Hulayfah (now Abyar Ali), near Madinah, is the miqat the Prophet set for people coming from Madinah.
explain.islamic-gk-7500: The 11th, 12th and 13th of Dhul-Hijjah are called Ayyam al-Tashriq, the days after Eid al-Adha spent at Mina.

explain.islamic-gk-7507: Tawaf al-Wada is the farewell circling of the Kaaba a pilgrim performs before leaving Makkah.
explain.islamic-gk-7510: The Prophet performed his only Hajj, the Farewell Hajj, in 10 AH, a few months before his death in 11 AH.
explain.islamic-gk-7566: Abu Bakr is first among the ten Companions (al-Asharah al-Mubashsharah) promised Paradise in the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf.
explain.islamic-gk-7567: Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, the Prophet's wife, was the first person and first woman to accept Islam.

explain.islamic-gk-7570: Zayd ibn Harithah, the Prophet's freed slave and adopted son, is traditionally counted as the first freed slave to accept Islam.
explain.islamic-gk-7571: Sumayyah bint Khayyat, mother of Ammar ibn Yasir, was killed by Abu Jahl for her faith and is counted as the first martyr of Islam.
explain.islamic-gk-7578: The Prophet sent Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah with his letter to al-Muqawqis, ruler of Egypt.
explain.islamic-gk-7580: Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri carried the Prophet's letter to the Negus (Najashi) of Abyssinia.
explain.islamic-gk-7677: Sahihayn ('the two Sahihs') refers to Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the two most authentic hadith collections.
explain.islamic-gk-7743: The Hanafi school is named after Imam Abu Hanifa al-Nu'man ibn Thabit (d. 150 AH) of Kufa.
explain.islamic-gk-7747: The Shafi'i school is named after Imam Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i (d. 204 AH).
explain.islamic-gk-7749: The Hanbali school is named after Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (d. 241 AH) of Baghdad.
explain.islamic-gk-7753: Al-Risalah, written by Imam al-Shafi'i, is regarded as the first systematic work on usul al-fiqh.
explain.islamic-gk-7755: Kitab al-Kharaj, a treatise on taxation and public finance, was written by Qadi Abu Yusuf for the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid.

explain.islamic-gk-7849: Surah An-Nisa (4:1) says Allah created mankind from a single soul (nafs wahidah), affirming the common origin of all humans.
explain.islamic-gk-7889: The hadith continues that every shepherd is answerable for his flock, making each person responsible and accountable for those in his charge.
explain.islamic-gk-7909: Hisbah was the office of the muhtasib, who inspected markets for fair weights and prices and enforced public morals and civic duties.
explain.islamic-gk-7911: The Mazalim courts heard grievances against officials and powerful people that ordinary qadi courts could not easily redress.
explain.islamic-gk-7969: Al-Itqan fi Ulum al-Quran is the well-known encyclopaedia of Quranic sciences by Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti (d. 1505).
explain.islamic-gk-7974: Mafatih al-Ghayb, also called al-Tafsir al-Kabir, is the major Quran commentary of Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi.
explain.islamic-gk-7975: Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, known as Tafsir Ibn Kathir, was written by the Damascene scholar Ismail ibn Kathir (d. 1373).

explain.islamic-gk-7982: Al-Hawi (Kitab al-Hawi fi al-Tibb, the Continens) is the vast medical compendium of the physician Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi.
explain.islamic-gk-7983: Kitab al-Manazir (Book of Optics) was written by Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen), founder of experimental optics.
explain.islamic-gk-7988: Al-Muqaddimah is Ibn Khaldun's introduction to his universal history Kitab al-Ibar, famous for its theory of society and history.
explain.islamic-gk-7989: Tarikh al-Rusul wal-Muluk (History of Prophets and Kings) is the universal history of Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari.
explain.islamic-gk-7994: Kashf al-Mahjub, the earliest Persian treatise on Sufism, was written by Ali al-Hujwiri (Data Ganj Bakhsh) of Lahore.
explain.islamic-gk-7996: Maktubat-e-Imam Rabbani is the collection of letters of Shaykh Ahmad Sirhindi, known as Mujaddid Alf Thani and Imam Rabbani.

explain.islamic-gk-8059: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan launched the Aligarh Movement and founded the MAO College at Aligarh in 1875 to promote modern education among Muslims.
explain.islamic-gk-8060: The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam is a collection of Allama Muhammad Iqbal's lectures, first published in 1930.
explain.islamic-gk-8061: Introduction to Islam is the widely translated book by Dr Muhammad Hamidullah.
explain.islamic-gk-8063: Caliph al-Mamun (813–833) patronised the Bayt al-Hikmah and sponsored translations of Greek works, marking the peak of the translation movement.
explain.islamic-gk-8069: Mosques, madrasas and hospitals were typically financed by waqf, a perpetual charitable endowment of property.
explain.islamic-gk-8070: In classical Islamic culture adab meant refined manners and conduct together with literary learning expected of a cultured person.
explain.islamic-gk-8072: In the Muqaddimah, Ibn Khaldun uses asabiyyah for group solidarity or social cohesion, the force behind the rise of dynasties.
explain.islamic-gk-8073: Amir Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan founded the Umayyad caliphate in 661 CE (41 AH).
explain.islamic-gk-8074: Muawiyah, who had been governor of Syria, made Damascus the capital of the Umayyad caliphate.
explain.islamic-gk-8078: The Abbasids defeated the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II at the Battle of the Zab and took power in 750 CE.
explain.islamic-gk-8079: Abu al-Abbas Abdullah al-Saffah was proclaimed the first Abbasid caliph in 750 CE; al-Mansur was his brother and successor.
explain.islamic-gk-8110: Basra, founded as a garrison town under Caliph Umar, became the home of the Basran school of Arabic grammar (Sibawayh, al-Khalil).
explain.islamic-gk-8111: Hazrat Ali moved the seat of the caliphate from Madinah to Kufa in 656 CE.
explain.islamic-gk-8141: The Abbasid dawah found its strongest early base in Khurasan, where Abu Muslim raised the black banners in 747 CE.
explain.islamic-gk-8148: The Abbasids descended from al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's uncle, and based their claim on this kinship.
explain.islamic-gk-8151: Al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762 CE and officially named it Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace.
explain.islamic-gk-8172: Al-Mustasim Billah was the last Abbasid caliph of Baghdad, killed when the Mongols sacked the city in 1258.
explain.islamic-gk-8173: The Mongol army that captured and sacked Baghdad in 1258 was led by Hulagu Khan, grandson of Chengiz Khan.
explain.islamic-gk-8190: The Mamluks, a ruling class of former military slaves, took power in Egypt in 1250, ending Ayyubid rule.
explain.islamic-gk-8191: At Ayn Jalut in Palestine in 1260 the Mamluks defeated the Mongols, halting their advance into Syria and Egypt.
explain.islamic-gk-8192: Baybars, a leading commander at Ayn Jalut, became Mamluk sultan in 1260 after Sultan Qutuz was killed.
explain.islamic-gk-8203: Nizam al-Mulk, vizier of the Seljuk sultans Alp Arslan and Malik Shah, founded the Nizamiyyah colleges, including the one in Baghdad (1067).
explain.islamic-gk-8204: Imam Abu Hamid al-Ghazali taught at the Nizamiyyah of Baghdad and later wrote Ihya Ulum al-Din.
explain.islamic-gk-8210: Salah al-Din ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 and founded the Ayyubid dynasty in Egypt.
explain.islamic-gk-8211: Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi defeated the Crusaders at Hattin in 1187 and recovered Jerusalem the same year.
explain.islamic-gk-8214: The Nizamiyyah colleges were founded under the Seljuk dynasty by their vizier Nizam al-Mulk.
explain.islamic-gk-8215: The Bayt al-Hikmah (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad, patronised especially by al-Mamun, was the centre of Abbasid translation and scholarship.
explain.islamic-gk-8218: Surah Al-Baqarah (2:143) calls Muslims ummatan wasatan, a balanced, justly moderate community that bears witness over mankind.

explain.islamic-gk-8234: Maqasid al-Shariah are the higher objectives of Islamic law, classically the protection of religion, life, intellect, lineage and property.
explain.islamic-gk-8236: The first revelation, the opening verses of Surah Al-Alaq, came to the Prophet (PBUH) in the Cave of Hira on Jabal al-Nur.
explain.islamic-gk-8254: Wahy is the divine revelation or communication from Allah to His prophets, most often through the angel Jibril.
explain.islamic-gk-8384: The barid was the state postal service of the caliphate, whose officers also sent intelligence reports on provinces to the capital.
explain.islamic-gk-8398: The Quran was revealed over about 23 years, roughly 13 years in Makkah and 10 in Madinah.
explain.mpt-course-english-d10q10: "Have to" is used for obligations imposed from outside, such as a departmental rule, while "must" usually carries the speaker's own authority.
explain.mpt-course-english-d10q2: Since he was on leave all week, it is logically impossible that he signed; "can't have + past participle" expresses this certainty about the past.
explain.mpt-course-english-d10q4: "Need not have + past participle" means an action was done but was unnecessary, which fits paying a fine that had been withdrawn.
explain.mpt-course-english-d10q5: Two modals cannot be used together, so "will can apply" is wrong; it should be "will be able to apply".
explain.mpt-course-english-d10q6: A past condition with a present result is a mixed conditional, using "would + base verb" in the result clause.
explain.mpt-course-english-d10q9: In a formal third conditional, "if" can be dropped by inverting "had": Had the funds been released on time...
explain.mpt-course-english-d11q10: The accounts receive the action, so the present simple passive "are audited" is needed.
explain.mpt-course-english-d11q2: The past perfect active "had issued" becomes "had been issued" in the passive.
explain.mpt-course-english-d11q3: An imperative sentence is changed to the passive with "Let + object + be + past participle".
explain.mpt-course-english-d11q4: The impersonal passive of a reporting verb uses "It is + past participle + that": It is alleged that...
explain.mpt-course-english-d11q6: The causative form is have + object + past participle: I had my car repaired.
explain.mpt-course-english-d11q7: With a two-object verb such as "send", the person can become the passive subject: the applicant was sent a notice.
explain.mpt-course-english-d12q1: A reported yes/no question uses "whether" or "if" with statement word order, and the tense shifts back: whether I had seen.
explain.mpt-course-english-d12q10: "Let us" (a proposal) is reported with "suggest": He suggested that the meeting should be postponed.
explain.mpt-course-english-d12q3: A negative command is reported with not + to-infinitive: 'warned us not to touch the exhibits'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d12q4: In reported speech a past simple action is backshifted to the past perfect, matching 'the previous day': 'had submitted'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d12q6: A permanent or universal truth keeps the present tense even after a past reporting verb: 'the sun rises in the east'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d12q8: A polite request with 'please' is reported as request + object + to-infinitive: 'He requested her to lend him her notes'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d13q1: 'One of the + superlative' must be followed by a plural noun, so 'the most competent officer' should be 'the most competent officers'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d13q10: 'A few' means some (a small number), and 'last' specifies one particular question, so it takes 'the'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d13q4: 'Prison' used for its purpose (as an inmate) takes no article, while 'the appeal' refers to the particular appeal in this case.
explain.mpt-course-english-d13q5: Pakistan is a single-word country name and takes no article, whereas 'the United Nations' and 'the Commonwealth' do.
explain.mpt-course-english-d13q7: 'Honour' begins with a silent h, so it takes 'an'; the relative clause 'that drafted the policy' identifies a specific committee, so 'the' is needed.
explain.mpt-course-english-d14q10: Adding a noun ('This delay') makes clear exactly what 'This' refers to; a bare 'This' is vague.
explain.mpt-course-english-d14q4: 'Whose' shows possession (the scholar's work); 'who's' means 'who is'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d14q6: A reflexive pronoun cannot be the subject; it should be 'Two colleagues and I prepared the draft'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d15q1: The participle phrase 'Driving through the flooded district' dangles because the bridges were not driving; the subject must be the person driving.
explain.mpt-course-english-d15q10: 'Only' should be placed next to what it limits, the timing: 'would sign the file only after the legal branch had cleared it'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d15q2: 'Almost' modifies the quantity 'all the funds', so it must stand directly before 'all'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d16q2: The noun 'solution' takes the preposition 'to': a solution to a problem.
explain.mpt-course-english-d16q5: The noun 'effect' takes 'on': an effect on something.
explain.mpt-course-english-d16q8: 'On time' means punctual, while 'in time' means early enough to do something.
explain.mpt-course-english-d17q1: 'Suggest' is followed by a gerund (or a that-clause), not a to-infinitive: 'suggested reconsidering'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d17q10: 'Manage' is followed by a to-infinitive: 'managed to submit'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d17q2: 'Stop + -ing' means to give up an activity, so 'stopped smoking' means he quit; 'stop + to' means to pause in order to do something.
explain.mpt-course-english-d17q3: 'Regret to inform' is used when announcing bad news now; 'regret informing' would mean being sorry about having informed someone earlier.
explain.mpt-course-english-d17q4: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund, not an infinitive: 'denied having received'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d17q5: The perfect participle 'Having examined' shows the examination came first, and its doer is the auditor, the subject of the main clause.
explain.mpt-course-english-d17q7: A gerund can act as the subject of a sentence, and 'Drafting' parallels the gerund 'enforcing' after 'than'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d17q9: The note was written in haste, so the past participle 'Written' correctly describes the subject 'the note'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d18q3: In a negative comparison of equality the pattern is 'not so … as'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d18q5: The correlative comparative pattern is 'the + comparative …, the + comparative': 'The sooner …, the better'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d19q10: 'As' already expresses the cause, so adding 'so' is redundant; the sentence should read 'As the rains failed, the wheat output fell'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d19q2: A noun phrase ('a shortage of funds') follows, so a prepositional connector like 'owing to' is needed; 'because' would need 'of'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d19q3: In 'not only … but also' both parts must have the same structure, so 'for revenue' must be matched by 'for excise'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d19q8: A full clause with its own subject ('small farmers could obtain credit') follows, so the conjunction 'so that' is required; 'in order to' and 'so as to' take a verb.
explain.mpt-course-english-d19q9: 'Whereas' is used to contrast two facts that are true at the same time; the other connectors show result, addition or cause.
explain.mpt-course-english-d1q10: A singular countable noun like 'decision' needs a determiner, so the sentence should begin 'The decision'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d1q2: 'Complaints' is a countable plural noun, so it takes 'number'; 'amount' and 'quantity' are used with uncountable nouns.
explain.mpt-course-english-d1q3: 'Performed' is an action verb, so it is modified by the adverb 'well', not the adjective 'good'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d1q5: An adverb is needed to modify the participle 'criticised', so 'sharply' is correct.
explain.mpt-course-english-d1q6: In 'Donors will fund the second phase', 'fund' follows the modal 'will' and expresses the action, so it is a verb; in the other options it is a noun.
explain.mpt-course-english-d1q8: 'Appear' is a linking verb here, so it is followed by an adjective ('convincing'), not an adverb.
explain.mpt-course-english-d1q9: 'Hard' means with great effort, while 'hardly' means almost not; he worked hard and hardly took any leave.
explain.mpt-course-english-d20q10: All three points begin with a gerund (improving, training, reducing), so the list is grammatically parallel.
explain.mpt-course-english-d20q6: Both sides of the comparison use the same form, a gerund phrase: 'Drafting a summary … drafting a note'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d20q7: 'Either … or' must join matching elements; after 'either submit' the second part should be 'or attach', without repeating 'they should'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d20q8: Both clauses are in the active voice, so the voice is consistent; the other options mix active and passive or are ungrammatical.
explain.mpt-course-english-d20q9: The list must be parallel: 'for planning, for budgeting and for monitoring', not 'to monitor'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d21q1: A colon should not separate a verb from its object; 'performs four functions' should not be interrupted by a colon.
explain.mpt-course-english-d21q3: When list items already contain commas (city, province), the items should be separated by semicolons.
explain.mpt-course-english-d21q5: No comma is needed between 'as' and the quoted phrase that completes it: 'described the delay as "wholly unexplained"'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d21q7: A semicolon joins two independent clauses; 'although the funds had been released in time' is a dependent clause, so a comma (or nothing) is correct.
explain.mpt-course-english-d21q9: A parenthetical insertion opened with a dash must be closed with a matching dash, not a comma.
explain.mpt-course-english-d22q2: History is by definition about the past, so 'past history' is redundant.
explain.mpt-course-english-d22q4: 'Each and every' repeats the same idea; 'each' or 'every' alone is enough.
explain.mpt-course-english-d22q6: 'In the event that' means simply 'if', so 'if the appeal is dismissed' is the concise equivalent.
explain.mpt-course-english-d22q7: 'Return' already means to send or come back, so 'returned back' is redundant.
explain.mpt-course-english-d22q8: 'The policy has had a limited effect' keeps the full meaning, including the qualification 'limited', without padding.
explain.mpt-course-english-d22q9: 'At this point in time' is a wordy way of saying 'now'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d23q1: 'Continual' means repeated with interruptions, which contradicts 'unbroken'; 'continuous' means without a break.
explain.mpt-course-english-d23q10: 'Establish the cause of the delay' is formal in register; the other options are informal or colloquial.
explain.mpt-course-english-d23q3: To 'infer' is to draw a conclusion from evidence; the press drew a conclusion, while a speaker 'implies'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d23q4: 'Comprise' is not followed by 'of': 'The committee comprises seven members' (or 'is composed of').
explain.mpt-course-english-d23q9: In British English 'practise' is the verb and 'practice' is the noun, so 'should practise' and 'regular practice'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d24q1: The second sentence begins with 'That judgement', picking up the idea that ended the first sentence, which links the two smoothly.
explain.mpt-course-english-d24q2: The sentence begins with the third person ('A candidate') but shifts to the second person ('you'); the person should stay consistent.
explain.mpt-course-english-d24q3: The summary noun 'refusal' names exactly what the previous sentence described, linking the two sentences precisely.
explain.mpt-course-english-d24q4: A topic sentence states one clear, arguable claim that the paragraph will support, as 'Enforcement, not legislation, is the binding constraint' does.
explain.mpt-course-english-d24q6: In 'the second, less so' the repeated words 'proposal was' are understood, which is correct ellipsis.
explain.mpt-course-english-d24q7: 'Moreover' signals addition, but the real link between the funds lapsing and the work stopping is cause and effect.
explain.mpt-course-english-d24q9: 'This' could refer to the ignored reminders or the missed deadline, so its reference is vague; a noun such as 'This failure' is needed.
explain.mpt-course-english-d25q10: The sentence uses British spellings ('programme', 'defence'), so 'analyse' should be used for consistency.
explain.mpt-course-english-d25q5: 'Eminent' means distinguished, describing the economist; 'imminent' means about to happen, describing the collapse.
explain.mpt-course-english-d25q8: 'Latter' refers to the second of two things mentioned; 'later' refers to time.
explain.mpt-course-english-d26q1: The subject's head noun is 'The number', which is singular, so the verb must be 'has exceeded'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d26q10: Replacing 'would have' with 'had' gives 'If I had known', the smallest change that corrects the conditional.
explain.mpt-course-english-d26q2: The subject is 'The quality', which is singular, so only 'were' needs changing to 'was'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d26q3: A period of time takes 'for', not 'since': 'for the last five years'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d26q5: With 'neither … nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject; 'officers' is plural, so 'were' is required.
explain.mpt-course-english-d26q6: 'Suggest' takes a gerund, so changing only 'to postpone' to 'postponing' is the minimum correction.
explain.mpt-course-english-d26q7: The comparison must be between like things: the population of Karachi and 'that of Lahore', not Lahore itself.
explain.mpt-course-english-d26q9: The participle 'Having reviewed the file' has no logical doer because 'a decision' cannot review a file; a person must be the subject.
explain.mpt-course-english-d2q3: A gerund phrase ('Improving literacy rates in rural districts') acts as a singular subject, so it takes 'requires'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d2q5: 'The budget was approved in March' has a subject and a finite verb and is not introduced by a subordinating word, so it is complete.
explain.mpt-course-english-d2q6: A what-clause used as a subject is treated as singular, so it takes 'is'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d2q8: 'Void' describes the direct object 'the contract' after the verb 'declared', so it is an object complement.
explain.mpt-course-english-d2q9: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'members', which is plural, so 'were'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d3q1: 'Even though' already introduces the contrast, so 'but' is redundant and should be deleted.
explain.mpt-course-english-d3q4: 'Because of' is followed by a noun phrase; a full clause ('the applicant had submitted …') needs 'because'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d3q5: 'Since' makes the clause dependent, so 'Since the deadline passed last Monday' cannot stand alone as a sentence.
explain.mpt-course-english-d3q6: The that-clause answers 'shows what?', so it is a noun clause acting as the object of 'shows'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d3q7: A non-defining relative clause set off by commas is introduced by 'which', not 'that'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d3q8: A full clause follows, so the conjunction 'While' is needed; 'during', 'despite' and 'in spite of' are followed by nouns.
explain.mpt-course-english-d5q4: In this inverted sentence the subject is 'three certificates', which is plural, so the verb is 'are'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d5q6: With 'most of', the verb agrees with the noun that follows; 'evidence' is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb, 'is'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d5q9: With 'either … or' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'deputies', which is plural, so 'have'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d6q4: 'And adopted a new flag' shares the subject 'Pakistan' and is not a separate clause, so no comma is needed before 'and'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d7q10: 'Contain' is a stative verb and is not normally used in continuous forms, so the simple present 'contains' is correct.
explain.mpt-course-english-d7q4: The present simple is conventionally used to describe what a literary work says or depicts: 'The novel describes'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d8q10: The present perfect is used with an unfinished time period such as 'this month', not with finished times like 'yesterday', 'last month' or 'in 2019'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d8q4: 'Since' with a period up to now requires the present perfect, and 'rise' is the intransitive verb (prices rise; someone raises prices).
explain.mpt-course-english-d8q6: 'How long' with an action that started in the past and continues now takes the present perfect continuous: 'have you been waiting'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d8q9: 'Lie' (to be in a position) has the past tense 'lay'; 'laid' is the past of 'lay' (to put something down) and 'lied' means told a lie.
explain.mpt-course-english-d9q1: In a first conditional the if-clause takes the present simple, not 'will': 'If the assembly passes the bill'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d9q10: When the reporting verb is in the past, 'will' in the original promise becomes 'would'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d9q3: The present continuous with a definite time ('at eleven tomorrow') expresses a fixed, planned arrangement.
explain.mpt-course-english-d9q5: The future continuous ('will be writing') describes an action in progress at a stated future time.
explain.mpt-course-english-d9q7: A scientific fact stays in the present tense even after a past reporting verb: 'light travels faster than sound'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d9q8: 'By the time' + a future event requires the future perfect for the earlier action: 'will have retired'.
explain.mpt-course-english-d9q9: 'Be going to' expresses an intention or plan decided before the moment of speaking.

explain.science-2371: The nucleolus, inside the nucleus, makes rRNA and assembles ribosomal subunits.
explain.science-2374: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes; it synthesises lipids and detoxifies drugs and poisons.
explain.science-2376: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that work at acidic pH to digest material inside the cell.
explain.science-2377: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and use catalase to decompose hydrogen peroxide.
explain.science-2378: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration and produce most of the cell's ATP.
explain.science-2379: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
explain.science-2380: The large central vacuole of a plant cell stores water and presses the cytoplasm against the wall, keeping the cell turgid.
explain.science-2381: The centrosome is the main microtubule-organising centre in animal cells and forms the spindle during division.
explain.science-2770: Xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots to the leaves.
explain.science-2851: Archaea are single-celled prokaryotes that form a separate domain of life from bacteria, differing in their membrane lipids and genetics.
explain.science-2853: Protozoa are mostly single-celled eukaryotes that obtain food by ingesting other organisms or organic matter, so they are heterotrophs.
explain.science-2855: Viroids are tiny circular RNA molecules with no protein coat that can infect plants, unlike viruses, which have a protein capsid.
explain.science-2856: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause normal proteins to misfold too, producing diseases such as mad cow disease.
explain.science-2857: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) carry out photosynthesis that releases oxygen, as plants do.
explain.science-2891: Cytotoxic (CD8+) T lymphocytes recognise viral antigens displayed on MHC class I molecules and trigger the death of infected cells.
explain.science-3175: Saturn has the largest and brightest ring system in the Solar System, made mostly of ice particles.
explain.science-3180: Europa is an icy moon of Jupiter, and magnetic-field and surface evidence suggests a salty liquid-water ocean beneath its ice shell.
explain.science-3251: In a lunar eclipse Earth lies between the Sun and the Moon, so Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
explain.science-3254: Spring tides happen when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up (at new and full moon), so the tidal pulls of the Sun and Moon add together.
explain.science-3255: Neap tides happen when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles to each other (at the quarter moons), so their tidal effects partly cancel.
explain.science-3257: At the northern winter solstice (around 21-22 December) the Northern Hemisphere is tilted furthest from the Sun, giving its shortest day.
explain.science-3261: Perigee is the point in the Moon's elliptical orbit where it is closest to Earth.
explain.science-3330: In the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, and this nuclear fusion releases the Sun's energy.
explain.science-4010: S (shear) waves need a rigid medium, and liquids cannot resist shear, so S waves cannot pass through Earth's liquid outer core.
explain.science-4290: Greenhouse gases such as water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, keeping Earth's surface warmer than it would otherwise be.
explain.science-4778: Human red blood cells live about 120 days before the spleen and liver remove them.
explain.science-4782: The Sun is a star, a ball of hot gas that produces its own light and energy through nuclear fusion.
explain.science-4784: Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust, making up about 46% of it by mass, mostly in silicate minerals.
explain.science-4787: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, at about 22.6 g/cm3, denser than platinum, copper or steel.
explain.science-4790: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium, so it travels through solids, liquids and gases but not through a vacuum.
explain.science-4798: Mercury is closest to the Sun and feels the strongest pull of its gravity, so it has the highest orbital speed, about 47 km/s.
explain.science-4820: Fats and oils are esters of glycerol and fatty acids, so they contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
explain.science-4831: A cardiograph (for example an electrocardiograph) records the activity and movements of the heart.
explain.science-4872: The mantle is about 2,900 km thick, which makes it the thickest of Earth's layers.
explain.science-4918: Producers such as green plants make their own food from carbon dioxide and water by photosynthesis.
explain.science-4947: Plant cells have a cell wall but animal cells have only a cell membrane; animal cells do have a nucleus, mitochondria and centrioles.
explain.science-4973: Amniotic fluid surrounds the foetus inside the amniotic sac and cushions it against shocks and mechanical injury.
explain.science-5010: A cyclone is a system of winds that spiral inward toward a centre of low pressure.
explain.science-5011: The International Energy Agency was set up in November 1974, after the 1973 oil crisis.
explain.science-5012: The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons has its headquarters in The Hague, in the Netherlands (Nederland).
explain.science-5014: The modern periodic table has 18 vertical columns (groups) and 7 horizontal rows (periods).
explain.science-5026: The sperm whale has the largest brain of any animal, weighing about 7-8 kg.
explain.science-5032: The African elephant has the largest ears of any animal, and it uses them to give off body heat.
explain.science-5034: The vertical columns of the periodic table are called groups; the horizontal rows are called periods.
explain.science-5064: The International Court of Justice sits in The Hague, Netherlands, while the UN's other principal organs are based in New York.
explain.science-5065: The International Atomic Energy Agency has its headquarters in Vienna, Austria.
explain.science-5080: Silver iodide is used in cloud seeding because its crystal structure resembles ice, so water droplets freeze on it and form precipitation.
explain.science-5089: The WWF logo shows a giant panda, based on Chi Chi, a panda at London Zoo.
explain.science-5119: A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a trait, which makes it the basic unit of heredity.
explain.science-5120: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the cell's energy currency, storing and releasing energy for cellular processes.
explain.science-5121: Secretin is a hormone released by the duodenum that makes the pancreas secrete bicarbonate, while pepsin and chymotrypsin are digestive enzymes.
explain.science-5126: Alzheimer's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder in which brain nerve cells (neurons) degenerate and die, causing memory loss.
explain.science-5144: Mumps is caused by the mumps virus, a paramyxovirus, and it causes swelling of the parotid salivary glands.
explain.science-5145: Insomnia is a sleep disorder in which a person persistently has difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep.
explain.science-5146: In medicine, TCM stands for Traditional Chinese Medicine, which includes practices such as acupuncture and herbal remedies.
explain.science-5148: Injecting heroin with shared needles can pass on HIV through infected blood, so it carries the highest HIV risk of the options.
explain.science-5149: Murine (endemic) typhus is transmitted to humans by rat fleas, whereas yellow fever is spread by mosquitoes.
explain.science-5150: Smallpox was caused by the variola virus, whereas cholera and tuberculosis are bacterial and malaria is caused by a protozoan.
explain.science-5151: Hysteria is a psychological condition and is not caused by an infectious agent, so it cannot pass from person to person.
explain.science-5152: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gums, usually caused by plaque building up on the teeth.
explain.science-5175: An adult human skeleton normally has 206 bones, because many bones present at birth fuse together.
explain.science-5176: The human heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles.
explain.science-5178: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills and one pumps it to the rest of the body.
explain.science-5179: Earthworms have no eyes; they detect light with photoreceptor cells in their skin.
explain.science-5248: The cerebrum is the largest part of the human brain and controls thought, voluntary movement and the senses.
explain.science-5251: An average adult human brain weighs about 1.2 to 1.4 kg.
explain.science-5253: The uvula is the small fleshy flap hanging from the back of the soft palate at the top of the throat.
explain.science-5254: Monocytes are the largest white blood cells, and in tissues they develop into macrophages.
explain.science-5268: The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat, controlling sweating, shivering and blood flow to keep body temperature steady.
explain.science-5269: In a camera the image is focused onto the film (or sensor), just as the eye's lens focuses the image onto the retina.
explain.science-5270: Bioluminescence is the production of light by living organisms, such as fireflies, through a chemical reaction involving luciferin.
explain.science-5291: Peristalsis is the wave-like contraction and relaxation of the oesophagus walls that pushes food down to the stomach.
explain.science-5303: Vitamin A is also called retinol, while thiamin is B1, riboflavin is B2 and ascorbic acid is vitamin C.
explain.science-5304: Pellagra, caused by a lack of niacin (vitamin B3), produces dermatitis, a skin inflammation, as one of its main symptoms.
explain.science-5305: Fats give about 9 kcal per gram, more than twice the roughly 4 kcal per gram from proteins or carbohydrates.
explain.science-5308: Pellagra is caused by a lack of niacin (vitamin B3) in the diet, while albinism is genetic and rabies is viral.
explain.science-5334: Phosphorus forms the phosphate groups in the sugar-phosphate backbone of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA).
explain.science-5341: Acetylsalicylic acid is the chemical name of aspirin, a common painkiller and anti-inflammatory drug.
explain.science-5342: Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid and has a pH of about 1.5-3.5, much lower than that of bile, saliva or pancreatic juice.
explain.science-5343: Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery in 1865 by using carbolic acid (phenol) to sterilise wounds and instruments.
explain.science-5398: Quartz is a mineral made of silicon dioxide (SiO2).
explain.science-5405: Half-life is the time for half of a radioactive sample to decay, so going from 10 mg to 5 mg takes one half-life, 8 days.
explain.science-5416: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, and the atomic number is the number of protons.
explain.science-5436: Charles's law states that at constant pressure the volume of a fixed amount of gas is directly proportional to its absolute (Kelvin) temperature.
explain.science-5437: Tungsten melts at about 3,422 °C, the highest melting point of any metal and far above silver, copper or iron.
explain.science-5441: Soap is made by saponification of fats, and sodium stearate, the sodium salt of stearic acid, is a typical soap.
explain.science-5442: Turning water into steam is a physical change of state, because no new substance is formed.
explain.science-5450: Cadmium's natural isotopes are stable, while uranium, radium and thorium are radioactive.
explain.science-5451: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere, and these break down ozone molecules.
explain.science-5485: Potential difference (voltage) is the work done in moving a unit charge between two points, measured in volts (joules per coulomb).
explain.science-5495: Dry wood is an electrical insulator, whereas copper and iron are metallic conductors and ordinary water with dissolved salts conducts better than dry wood.
explain.science-5523: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles, not a form of energy itself; heat, light and electricity are forms of energy.
explain.science-5547: Average speed is defined as total distance travelled divided by the time taken; it equals the magnitude of average velocity only when motion is in a straight line without reversal.
explain.science-5555: The Earth's gravity pulls the gases of the atmosphere towards the planet and prevents them from escaping into space.
explain.science-5558: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and highest frequency in the electromagnetic spectrum, so their photons carry the most energy.
explain.science-5559: Coal is a fossil fuel formed over millions of years and cannot be replenished on a human timescale, while hydro, wind and solar energy are renewable.
explain.science-5572: The magnifying power of a simple microscope is M = 1 + D/f, so a lens of shorter focal length gives greater magnification.
explain.science-5589: A photometer is an instrument used to measure the intensity of light (luminous intensity or illuminance).
explain.science-5591: White light passing through a prism disperses into seven colours: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red (VIBGYOR).
explain.science-5593: Astigmatism is caused by unequal curvature of the cornea or lens, and it is corrected with cylindrical lenses that focus light differently in different planes.
explain.science-5594: In short-sightedness (myopia) the image forms in front of the retina, so a concave (diverging) lens is used to correct it.
explain.science-5595: Infrared radiation has a longer wavelength than visible light, ultraviolet and X-rays, which lie at progressively shorter wavelengths.
explain.science-5596: The Danish astronomer Ole Roemer made the first measurement of the speed of light in 1676 by observing the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io; Galileo's earlier attempt failed.
explain.science-5609: Ammonia consists of one nitrogen atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms, so its formula is NH3.
explain.science-5611: In the SI system the unit of length is the metre, so the unit of volume is the cubic metre (m³).
explain.science-5612: The foot-candle is a unit of illuminance (light falling on a surface), whereas the astronomical unit, parsec and light year are units of distance.
explain.science-5633: Vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium and phosphorus; its deficiency in children softens the bones and causes rickets.
explain.science-5636: In the Sun's core hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, and this nuclear fusion releases the Sun's energy.
